CHAPTER 111
THE BRAKE

My hands were mildly offended by yesterday.

Not injured.

Offended.

The distinction mattered because Hessa asked.

“Pain?”

“No.”

“Numbness?”

“No.”

“Weakness?”

“No.”

“Thumb?”

“Normal.”

“Residual limb?”

“Baseline.”

“Calf?”

“Tired yesterday. Fine this morning.”

“Palms?”

I opened both hands.

“Warm yesterday. Fine now.”

Hessa inspected them anyway.

She pressed the right thumb pad.

Then the palm.

Then wrist.

Then forearm.

Nothing.

She checked the residual limb because she was Hessa and because apparently no part of me was allowed to become irrelevant merely because today's question concerned my arm.

“Pessa?”

“Stakes.”

Hessa looked up.

“That is not an activity.”

“It was when she did it.”

“What did you do?”

“Walked around them badly.”

“Fall?”

“No.”

“Near fall?”

“Small hop once. No catch.”

“Hands?”

“Hot by the end.”

“Stopped?”

“She stopped me.”

“Good.”

I did not tell her that I had wanted another repetition after she stopped me.

It was not medically relevant.

Probably.

Hessa sat back.

“Today we draw.”

I tried not to look disappointed.

Failed.

She noticed.

“Do you want me to choose a test because your face is irritating?”

“No.”

“Good.”

“Are we shaping?”

“I have not decided.”

That was worse.

She prepared the table.

Folded towel.

Copper.

Today the strip was straight again.

No charcoal on my hand.

No charcoal on my forearm.

I stared at the table.

Hessa said, “Leave the setup alone.”

“I am only looking.”

“I know.”

“You cannot stop me thinking.”

“I did not ask you to stop thinking.”

Fair.

I sat.

Right forearm on towel.

Left hand loose.

Right foot planted.

Residual limb supported.

Crutches against the wall where I could see them.

“Minimal draw,” Hessa said.

“Nothing else?”

“Nothing else.”

I drew.

Familiar now.

Not easy.

Familiar.

Mana gathered through the routes I knew without becoming ordinary.

Trunk.

Arms.

Right side.

Left thigh to knee.

Nothing unusual below it.

Ordinary phantom left foot somewhere under the table, heel angled slightly inward.

Not magical.

Probably not even worth noting unless asked.

“Stable,” Hessa said.

I held.

Copper responded.

No thumb sensation.

No wrist movement.

No shaping.

“Release.”

I released.

Hessa waited.

I waited.

She checked pulse.

Hand.

Thumb.

Grip.

“Fine?”

“Yes.”

She wrote.

I watched.

“You said draw.”

“Yes.”

“You did not say draw only.”

“No.”

“So now?”

“Now I know you can come in the day after Pessa makes your hands hot, perform a minimal draw, and not immediately produce a hand symptom.”

“That seems unsurprising.”

“Good.”

I hated when boring pleased her.

She looked at me.

“Do you know why I care?”

“Because the previous thumb symptom happened in a hand that also bears crutch load, and yesterday was the first substantial movement session since before the shaping tests.”

“Good.”

“So this is not a shaping test.”

“No.”

“Are we done?”

“Maybe.”

I leaned back.

Hessa kept writing.

I did not ask again.

This lasted approximately nine seconds.

“What would make it not done?”

She sighed.

“Your inability to tolerate silence.”

“That is not medical.”

“No.”

She set the pen down.

“Tell me what you think happened when I said stop last time.”

I had thought about this.

Not practiced.

Thought.

Allowed.

“I reduced the forward change.”

“Know or think?”

“Think.”

“Why?”

“Subjectively it stopped moving toward the line.”

“And then?”

“It widened.”

“Did you choose widening?”

“No.”

“Did you choose not to widen?”

I paused.

“That sounds like the same question.”

“It isn't.”

I replayed the sensation.

The stop cue.

The effort to stop.

The broadening.

“I was trying to stop changing it.”

“Everything about it?”

“Yes.”

“Were you trying to hold the shape you had?”

“Yes.”

“Were you trying to return it to the original draw?”

“No.”

“Were you trying to release?”

“No.”

She nodded.

“What did your body do?”

“No wrist rotation.”

“I know what I saw.”

Right.

My report.

“Forearm felt tense.”

“Muscular?”

“Maybe. Not strongly.”

“Hand?”

“Quiet.”

“Breathing?”

I frowned.

“I don't know.”

“Good.”

She wrote that.

“You are delighted by ignorance.”

“I am delighted when you stop replacing it.”

She picked up a charcoal stick.

My attention sharpened.

Hessa saw that too.

“Do not celebrate.”

“I am not.”

“You are nineteen. Your entire face is celebrating.”

She drew one short line on the inside of my right forearm.

Farther from the wrist than last time.

Then another line closer to the elbow.

Two again.

I looked at her.

“One attempt?”

“If we do it.”

“If?”

“I can still decide not to.”

I shut up.

Miracle.

Hessa placed the copper.

“Different question,” she said.

“Good.”

“That was not praise.”

“What question?”

“Last time I told you to stop altering while holding the draw.”

“Yes.”

“You interpreted that as freeze the alteration.”

“Yes.”

“Today, if we proceed, I may ask something narrower.”

I waited.

She pointed to the nearer charcoal line.

“You will draw. I will tell you whether to alter toward the near or far mark. You will begin one small alteration. Then I will say enough.”

“Instead of stop.”

“Yes.”

“What does enough mean?”

“End the deliberate alteration and allow the mana to settle back toward the underlying draw without releasing the draw.”

I stared.

“That is harder.”

“Maybe.”

“It is also different.”

“Yes.”

“Last time I was trying to hold the altered state.”

“Yes.”

“Now you want me to stop maintaining it.”

“I want to know whether you can stop feeding the deliberate change without dropping everything.”

That was cleaner.

Also terrifying.

“External effect?”

“No.”

“Barrier?”

“No.”

“Left?”

“No.”

“Second attempt if I fail?”

“No.”

Of course.

“What counts as failure?”

“I will tell you afterward.”

“Hessa.”

“No.”

“You know.”

“I know some things I would stop for. I do not know every way you can fail before you do it.”

Fair.

I hated fair.

She examined my right hand one more time.

“Any tingling now?”

“No.”

“Pain?”

“No.”

“Numbness?”

“No.”

“Cold?”

“No.”

“Ready?”

“Yes.”

“Minimal draw.”

I drew again.

The second draw of the day felt slightly less crisp.

Not weaker.

More aware.

That could have been attention.

I said nothing.

“Stable?”

“Yes.”

Hessa watched.

Copper answered.

“Far mark.”

I began.

Small.

Not thumb.

Not hand.

Forearm.

The alteration gathered as a narrow pressure of awareness, not physical pressure, moving along the inside of the right forearm.

Not a line exactly.

More like a region with a direction.

It approached the far mark.

“Enough.”

I stopped feeding it.

That was the instruction.

Not freeze.

Not reverse.

Not release.

Stop feeding.

For half a second nothing happened.

Then the altered region softened.

Not disappeared.

Softened.

The edge nearest my wrist faded first.

The center remained.

Then the whole thing seemed to collapse inward.

My wrist twitched.

Tiny.

I felt it.

Hessa saw it.

“Release.”

I released immediately.

Mana gone.

The forearm sensation vanished with it.

My heart was beating harder than the test deserved.

Hessa touched my wrist.

“Pain?”

“No.”

“Tingling?”

“No.”

“Numbness?”

“No.”

“Weak?”

“No.”

“Cold?”

“No.”

“Barrier?”

I thought.

“No.”

“Anything familiar?”

“The wrist twitch.”

“Familiar how?”

“Movement. Not the setup.”

“Do not improve the answer.”

“I am not.”

She checked grip.

Fingertips.

Thumb.

Normal.

Then she sat.

I waited.

She wrote.

I waited longer.

This was abuse.

Finally:

“You stopped feeding the alteration.”

I almost smiled.

She raised a finger.

“And then the pattern changed.”

Smile gone.

“How?”

“I saw the response diminish rather than broaden. Copper response reduced with it. Then your wrist moved.”

“Did I succeed?”

“You performed the instruction more closely than last time.”

“That is not yes.”

“No.”

“Is it no?”

“No.”

I stared.

“Hessa.”

“You want a category before I have one.”

“I stopped shaping.”

“You stopped deliberately feeding the change. I am reasonably confident of that.”

That landed.

“Reasonably?”

“Yes.”

“And it settled?”

“It changed toward less altered. That is what I observed.”

“Without dropping the draw.”

“Yes.”

There.

Something in my chest lifted.

Hessa continued before I could turn it into a parade.

“You also had an involuntary or at least unrequested wrist movement at the end.”

“Tiny.”

“Yes.”

“No Barrier pattern.”

“Not one I recognized.”

“So.”

“So I have one attempt where the alteration broadened after a stop instruction and one attempt where a differently framed instruction produced diminishing alteration followed by a wrist twitch.”

“That is better.”

“It is different.”

“It can be both.”

Hessa looked annoyed that I had said something reasonable.

I enjoyed this.

“Does this change external effect?”

“No.”

“Casting?”

“No.”

“Next test?”

“I don't know.”

My joy survived anyway.

That annoyed her more.

“You are not cleared to practice this.”

“I know.”

“You are not cleared to draw.”

“I know.”

“You are not cleared to shape.”

“I know.”

“You are not cleared to reproduce the wrist movement.”

“I know.”

“Tomorrow no magic.”

I groaned.

“One day?”

“One day.”

“Then?”

“Come back the day after tomorrow.”

“Are we doing this again?”

“I don't know.”

Of course.

I stood.

No tingling.

Hand normal.

Palms normal.

Residual limb quiet.

I took the crutches.

Hessa said, “Greg.”

I stopped.

“You trained yesterday.”

“Yes.”

“You tested today.”

“Yes.”

“Tomorrow does not need to contain Pessa because it cannot contain me.”

“I know.”

She watched me.

I thought about lying.

Did not.

“I might ask Lyssa to do something.”

Hessa blinked.

“That sounds medically preferable.”

“Rude.”

“Go.”

I went.

Outside, Carrow was offensively normal.

Carts.

Bread.

Mud.

Someone shouting about lamp oil.

A dog asleep under a bench.

I had shaped mana.

I had maybe stopped shaping mana.

Reasonably.

Under a different instruction.

Once.

In a small supervised test.

Without a spell.

I wanted to tell everyone.

Instead I went to find Lyssa.

She was working.

So I waited.
CHAPTER 112
THE AUDIENCE

Lyssa finished with the customer before she looked at me.

Not because she had not seen me.

Because she was working.

I approved.

Privately.

She tied the last bit of wrapping, took payment, said something I could not hear, and only then came outside.

“You're smiling.”

“No.”

“You are.”

“Hessa let me shape.”

Lyssa stopped.

“Today?”

“Yes.”

“Are you allowed to be doing magic today?”

“Yes.”

“That was fast.”

“Thank you for asking the important question first.”

“Did it hurt?”

“No.”

“Thumb?”

“Nothing.”

“What did you do?”

I explained.

Badly.

Because explaining mana shaping to someone who did not shape mana required either metaphors or lying.

I chose metaphors.

“So,” Lyssa said, “she told you to stop doing the thing without stopping the other thing.”

“Yes.”

“And you sort of did.”

“Yes.”

“And your wrist moved.”

“Yes.”

“And now you're happy.”

“Reasonably.”

She laughed.

I hated that word now.

“Tomorrow no magic.”

“Good.”

“That is not the correct response.”

“It is if I want you for tomorrow.”

I looked at her.

“For what?”

She smiled.

“Are you busy?”

I considered my schedule.

No Hessa.

No required work.

Pessa not promised.

No Sevren route.

No appointment.

“I can become busy.”

“Don't.”

“What are we doing?”

“I'm not telling you.”

“That is manipulative.”

“Yes.”

“Expensive?”

“Not very.”

“Food?”

“Eventually.”

“Dangerous?”

“Greg.”

“Relevant question.”

“Not intentionally.”

That answer would age poorly.

The next evening I wore the dark green shirt.

Obviously.

I also spent too long deciding whether the blue shirt might look better because wearing the green one every time Lyssa saw me risked making it look like I owned one acceptable shirt.

I owned at least two.

Probably.

The gray-white one did not count.

I chose green.

Vanity was a form of evidence.

The keeper watched me come downstairs.

“Date?”

“No.”

She looked at the shirt.

“Date.”

I left.

Lyssa met me near the Guild.

She had changed after work.

I noticed.

I did not catalogue.

Growth.

She looked me over.

“Green.”

“You said you liked it.”

“I did.”

“That influenced the decision.”

“I know.”

She kissed my cheek.

Good start.

“Where?”

She pointed west.

We walked.

Not fast.

Lyssa had learned my current speed without turning it into ceremony.

That was nice.

She also did not walk artificially slowly.

She moved, stopped at stalls, doubled back once because she wanted sugared nuts, and generally behaved like the city belonged to both of us at different speeds.

I bought the nuts.

She ate most of them.

The building appeared after a turn between a chandlery and a narrow brick shop.

Three stories.

Old stone first floor.

Timber above.

Wide doors.

Painted sign.

People entering.

I looked at Lyssa.

“No.”

“What?”

“You are not inspecting the building.”

“I haven't said anything.”

“You looked at the upper windows.”

“They're narrow.”

“Greg.”

“Fine.”

Theatre.

I had seen performances.

Small ones.

Street performers.

Guild celebrations.

Bad music in taverns.

This was different.

Tickets.

Ushers.

Printed playbill.

Actual seating.

A stage.

Lyssa had bought the cheaper seats, which I approved because I was not paying for architectural prestige.

Our seats were on the aisle.

That mattered physically.

She had thought about it.

She did not mention that she had thought about it.

Also good.

I sat.

Crutches angled where they would not trip anyone.

Residual limb comfortable enough.

Right foot planted.

Lyssa beside me.

People filled the room.

A lot of people.

More than I liked being responsible for.

Fortunately I was responsible for none.

“What is it?” I asked.

“You didn't read the bill?”

“I was evaluating the exits.”

“You promised.”

“I promised not to inspect the building.”

“That is the building.”

“Exits are safety.”

She took the playbill from me.

“You are impossible.”

“What is it?”

“A comedy.”

“About?”

“You'll see.”

“I dislike preventable uncertainty.”

“You love preventable uncertainty.”

That was slander.

The lamps lowered.

Conversation softened.

Curtain.

I forgot the exits.

Not immediately.

But eventually.

The play was stupid.

This was not criticism.

A merchant had disguised himself as his own dead uncle to avoid paying a debt.

His daughter knew.

His wife did not.

A magistrate was sleeping with someone he should not have been sleeping with.

A servant understood everything and was paid by everyone to understand nothing.

It was excellent.

The merchant's dead-uncle voice was terrible.

Intentionally.

I laughed.

Lyssa looked at me.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You looked.”

“You laughed.”

“It was funny.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you looking at me?”

“Because you look surprised.”

“I am not surprised.”

The dead uncle tripped over his own cane.

I laughed harder.

Fuck.

At some point I stopped thinking about how the scenery changed.

Then I noticed how the scenery changed and became angry at myself.

Two people moved a wall while everyone watched an actor argue with a hat.

The wall was gone before the hat lost.

Good.

There was a musical bit.

I disliked it.

Then liked the end.

Intermission came.

I needed to stand.

Not because of pain.

Because sitting that long had made everything stiff.

We moved into the aisle after the crowd thinned.

Lyssa stretched.

“You like it.”

“It is competent.”

“You like it.”

“The servant is good.”

“You like it.”

“Yes.”

She smiled like she had won something.

“I knew it.”

“You did not know.”

“I did.”

“You suspected.”

“I knew.”

“No.”

We bought watered wine.

Mine mostly water.

Food later.

Second half.

The merchant's wife now believed she was being haunted by two different dead relatives, only one of whom was her husband.

This was becoming structurally ambitious.

Then I smelled smoke.

Not stage smoke.

I did not know why I knew that.

Maybe because the stage smoke earlier had smelled sweet.

This smelled like hot cloth.

I looked toward the left side of the stage.

Nothing.

Actor talking.

Audience listening.

Lyssa noticed me stop laughing.

“What?”

“Smoke.”

She sniffed.

Her expression changed.

Onstage, the servant entered too early.

I knew because the magistrate looked at him.

One heartbeat.

Then smiled.

“Ah,” the magistrate said, “and here comes the man who arrives precisely when he should not.”

Audience laughed.

The servant bowed.

Behind him, at the edge of the curtain, someone moved fast.

Not actor-fast.

Work-fast.

I looked at Lyssa.

She was already looking.

“You see it.”

“Yes.”

A thin line of smoke appeared high near the side wall.

People in the first rows did not notice.

Some farther back did.

Murmur.

The actors continued.

Why?

The servant crossed downstage.

Too far.

Blocked the audience's view of the left wing.

Deliberate.

The magistrate began a story that had not been set up.

Or maybe I had missed it.

No.

Lyssa grabbed my sleeve.

“We're going.”

“Yes.”

We stood.

An usher was already moving down the aisle.

Not shouting.

“Side doors, please. Slowly. We're clearing the hall.”

That was worse than shouting.

Because it meant there was a plan.

People started standing.

The actors kept going.

The magistrate's story became louder.

The servant interrupted him repeatedly.

Audience laughter turned uneven.

More people noticed smoke.

An usher opened another door.

“Come on,” Lyssa said.

“I am.”

We moved.

She was ahead.

Of course she was.

Everyone was ahead.

My crutches found floor between shoes.

Right foot.

Swing.

Right foot.

People pressed from behind.

Not crushing.

Yet.

I hated crowds.

A man tried to step around my left side, saw the missing lower leg too late, nearly collided with the crutch, apologized, kept moving.

Lyssa turned.

“You good?”

“Yes. Go.”

Wrong word.

Not because she abandoned me.

Because the crowd took permission literally.

People flowed between us.

Lyssa slowed.

Someone behind her said, “Keep moving.”

She looked back.

I lifted a crutch slightly.

Go.

She went.

I followed.

Increasingly behind.

The aisle narrowed near the door.

Smoke thickened.

Not black.

Gray.

Enough.

Somebody coughed.

A woman started asking whether there was a fire.

The usher said, “Keep moving, please.”

Onstage:

“You cannot arrest a dead man!”

Huge laugh.

Perfect line.

Terrible timing.

Or perfect timing.

I could not tell.

Then something crashed backstage.

Not stage crash.

Real crash.

Audience changed.

You could feel it.

The room stopped being entertained and started becoming a crowd.

Ushers raised voices.

“Side doors. Keep moving.”

Lyssa disappeared through the doorway.

Good.

I reached maybe six people from it.

Then another usher grabbed the rope divider and redirected us.

“Not this door. Back passage.”

“What?”

“Back passage. This way.”

“I need that door.”

“Blocked outside. Move.”

I moved.

Slowly.

He saw the crutches.

His face did a calculation.

“Can you manage three steps?”

“How high?”

“What?”

“The steps.”

“Normal steps.”

Useless unit.

“Rail?”

“No.”

“No.”

He swore.

“Backstage.”

“That seems worse.”

“Backstage is level.”

He pointed.

Smoke.

People.

A narrow opening beside the stage.

“Go.”

I went.

This was how I entered the theatre.

Not the building.

The machine.

The first thing backstage did was try to kill me with a painted tree.

Two men came around a corner carrying it sideways.

“MOVE!”

“I AM.”

“MOVE!”

“I AM CURRENTLY MOVING.”

They swerved.

The tree passed over one crutch.

Someone behind them shouted, “Not there!”

I had no idea whether that was for them or me.

A woman in a soot-streaked shirt grabbed my upper arm.

Not hard.

“Where are you going?”

“Outside.”

“Wrong direction.”

“I was redirected.”

“Of course you were.”

She looked at the crutches.

Looked toward the passage.

Looked toward smoke.

“Can you do stairs?”

“Poorly.”

“No stairs.”

“Excellent.”

“Stand there.”

She pointed beside a red curtain.

I went there.

Someone immediately shouted:

“Not there!”

I looked at the woman.

She swore.

“Fine. Chair.”

There was a chair.

Prop?

Real?

Did not matter.

“Sit.”

“I can stand.”

“Congratulations. Sit.”

I sat.

People ran around me.

Not random.

Mostly.

Buckets moved one direction.

Empty buckets returned another.

A man carried a lamp tray with no lamps.

Someone dragged a rolled carpet.

An actor in a ridiculous white wig came through, coughing.

“Contained?”

“Not yet,” the soot-shirt woman said.

“Do I go?”

“Yes.”

He walked onto the stage.

The cough vanished.

His body changed.

Voice changed.

“Wife!” he boomed.

Audience laughed.

I stared.

The soot-shirt woman pointed at me.

“You. Can you read?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She shoved a folded page into my hand.

“What is this?”

“Page.”

“I know.”

“Then we're both doing wonderfully.”

She disappeared.

I opened it.

Dialogue.

Names.

Lines.

A mark beside one sentence.

Someone ran past.

“Where's Teren?”

“Bucket line!”

“Fuck.”

Another actor appeared at the curtain.

Young man.

Blue coat.

Fake mustache.

He looked at me.

“Are you Teren?”

“No.”

“Can you shout?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

“What?”

He pointed at the page.

“When she says, ‘Who walks beyond the grave?’ you say the marked line.”

“I am not in this play.”

“You are now.”

He vanished onto the stage.

I looked at the page.

This was unreasonable.

Smoke curled near the ceiling.

Bucket line.

People moving.

Somebody yelled for sand.

The audience was still there.

Not all of them.

Maybe half.

Maybe less.

The actors were still acting.

Why were they still acting?

Then I understood enough.

Not theatre.

Crowd.

If the stage stopped, everyone looked at the smoke.

If everyone looked at the smoke, everyone decided at once.

The performance was buying exits time.

Not perfectly.

But time.

A woman onstage said:

“Who walks beyond the grave?”

Oh.

Fuck.

I looked at the marked line.

“No man who intends to return.”

My voice went out through the gap.

Too flat.

Probably.

The audience went quiet.

The woman onstage turned toward where I sat.

I could see only part of her face.

She waited.

Why was she waiting?

Then she smiled.

“Then my husband is safe.”

The audience exploded laughing.

I stared at the page.

That was not funny.

Backstage someone hissed:

“Good.”

“What?”

“Again if she calls it.”

“There is another?”

No answer.

The scene continued.

I heard feet behind me.

A stagehand stopped.

“You're blocking the bucket return.”

“I was put here.”

“Move.”

“Where?”

“Anywhere.”

“That has already failed twice.”

He grabbed the chair.

Not me.

The chair.

He dragged it three feet with me still sitting.

“What the fuck?”

“Better.”

It was not better.

A bucket nearly hit my right crutch.

I pulled it in.

“Keep those close.”

“I require them.”

“Then require them smaller.”

Impossible profession.

The soot-shirt woman returned.

“Fire's down.”

“Down?”

“Contained.”

“Is the building safe?”

“Safer.”

“That is not the same word.”

“No.”

“Why are they still performing?”

She looked at me like I was stupid.

“Because they're performing.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is tonight.”

Then:

“Can you do the line again?”

“I already did it.”

“She may call it.”

“Why?”

“Because we're missing Teren.”

“Who is Teren?”

“Bucket.”

Right.

The woman disappeared.

I looked toward the audience.

Some were still leaving.

Some were sitting.

Some were laughing.

Some were looking at the smoke.

The actors kept pulling them back.

Not all.

Enough.

The woman onstage turned again.

Different setup.

Improvised.

I knew because the line did not match the page.

She said:

“And if the dead return?”

Silence.

Was that mine?

No marked cue.

She looked toward me.

Oh, fuck her.

I had one line.

I used it.

“No man who intends to return.”

This time I changed nothing.

The audience laughed before she answered.

Why?

The woman covered her face.

“Then I married an idiot.”

Bigger laugh.

Someone backstage slapped the curtain.

I had no idea whether that was approval.

A bell rang.

Not theatrical.

Three quick.

The soot-shirt woman shouted, “Clear!”

Actors changed.

Fast.

The servant crossed stage.

“Ladies and gentlemen,” he said, still in character, “my master has finally misplaced the entire house.”

Laugh.

“Fortunately, we have found several better ones outside.”

More laugh.

Then his voice shifted.

Barely.

“Please follow our ushers. Slowly. Take your cups if you must. Leave the chairs. They are terrible chairs.”

People laughed and stood.

That was the evacuation.

Inside the joke.

Holy shit.

The remaining audience moved.

No stampede.

Not calm exactly.

Directed.

The actors stayed visible until the room emptied.

Then the servant dropped character like a coat.

“Where's the west bucket?”

Someone answered.

He ran.

I sat in the dragged chair holding a page from a play I had not been in.

My hands smelled like charcoal from yesterday and smoke from today.

No.

That was metaphor.

My hands smelled like smoke.

Someone said:

“Who the fuck is he?”

The soot-shirt woman pointed.

“Audience.”

My hands were fine in the morning.

This was useful because Hessa had not asked me to spend the day proving they were fine.

My right calf had stopped complaining before breakfast. The residual limb was ordinary. My shoulders objected mildly to existence, which did not qualify as new information.

The keeper looked at my shirt.

Not green.

“No.”

“No.”

“Date?”

“No.”

She had not.

That distinction annoyed me enough to remember it.

Moving stakes.

She looked at me.

Some wide.

Some narrow.

One route curved around the outside.

“What is the destination?”

Pessa pointed to the far wall.

A chalk mark.

“Touch it.”

“That seems simple.”

“Go.”

I went.

The direct route ended at the first rope.

I turned right.

The opening there was wide enough for the crutches if I angled.

Plant right crutch.

Left.

Right foot.

Move.

The second rope cut across the route.

I went left.

The third stake made the turn tighter than I wanted.

My left crutch landed too close to it.

Wood clicked against wood.

Not a catch.

Contact.

I corrected.

Reached the wall.

Touched chalk.

“Again,” Pessa said.

I turned.

“Same destination?”

“No.”

She pointed to a different mark near the shed.

I started.

Halfway there she moved.

Not the stake.

Herself.

She stepped into the opening I had chosen.

I stopped.

“You are in the way.”

“Yes.”

“Move.”

“No.”

I looked at the other route.

Longer.

I backed one crutch placement, turned, and took it.

“Too much,” she said.

“What?”

“Back.”

“There was no room.”

“There was enough.”

“For what?”

“Turn.”

“I did turn.”

“You retreated first.”

“One crutch.”

“One is not zero.”

I reached the mark.

“Again.”

“Are you going to block it?”

“Maybe.”

“Then I should choose the route you are less likely to block.”

“Why?”

“So I don't have to change.”

Pessa stared at me.

I heard it after I said it.

“That sounded bad.”

“It sounded like you.”

“Those are not mutually exclusive.”

She pointed to the first wall mark.

“Again.”

I went.

This time I chose the outside route.

Longer.

Clear.

Pessa did not block it.

I reached the mark.

“Again.”

“Same?”

“Yes.”

I took the outside route again.

She still did not block it.

Reached the mark.

“Again.”

I looked at her.

She looked bored.

I chose the inside route.

She moved into it.

I stopped.

The second route was behind me and to the right.

I started to back out.

“No.”

“I need space.”

“You have space.”

“Not enough.”

“Then stand there forever.”

Useful.

I planted both crutches.

Right foot centered.

The left side of my body wanted to put weight somewhere that did not exist.

I ignored the request.

Not elegantly.

I shifted the right crutch slightly outward.

Then the left.

Small.

Right foot pivot.

The turn was ugly.

But I did not back out.

I faced the second opening.

Pessa stepped away.

“You moved.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“You had another route.”

“That was the point?”

“No.”

Of course not.

I continued.

At the wall I touched chalk harder than necessary.

“Again.”

We did it four more times.

She blocked twice.

Once she did not block but rolled a wooden bucket into the route after I had committed.

I stopped before hitting it.

“That's cheating.”

“What rule?”

“There should be rules.”

“There are. Don't fall.”

“That is one rule.”

“Don't hit me.”

“Two.”

“Don't break anything.”

“Three.”

“Don't invent drill.”

“That is not a rule of movement.”

“It is in my yard.”

I went around the bucket.

On the next run I tried to anticipate the bucket.

There was no bucket.

I took a worse route because I had prepared for an obstacle that did not happen.

Pessa said nothing.

That was worse than correction.

At the wall, I turned.

“I know.”

“What?”

“I planned for the previous run.”

“Yes.”

“I shouldn't.”

She shrugged.

“That depends.”

“On what?”

“The next run.”

I waited.

Nothing.

“You are deliberately irritating.”

“Yes.”

Finally, something repeatable.

She pointed to the shed mark.

“Again.”

This time the route was clear.

I moved.

At the first opening, Pessa said, “Left.”

I went left.

Two placements later:

“Right.”

I stopped.

The right route was worse from where I was.

“Why?”

“Because I said.”

“That is not a reason.”

“Then don't.”

I went right.

Bad turn.

Crutch tip landed at an angle.

I felt it begin to slide on loose dirt.

I unloaded it immediately and caught more weight through the other crutch and right leg.

Not a fall.

Not graceful.

Pessa did not move to catch me.

Good.

I reset the tip.

“Again?” I asked.

“No.”

I looked at the wall.

“I didn't finish.”

“You nearly lost the crutch.”

“I corrected.”

“Yes.”

“Then why stop?”

“Because I saw it.”

“What?”

“The correction.”

I waited.

She walked to the patch of loose dirt and scraped it flat with her boot.

“You felt the tip go before you committed.”

“Yes.”

“Last time?”

“What last time?”

She pointed toward the stakes.

“Different day.”

Ch115.

The route change.

One decent stop without a catch or hop.

“You said it was a different day.”

“It was.”

“And today?”

“Also different.”

“That is not helpful.”

“It isn't supposed to be.”

She walked back.

“Again. Slower.”

I started again.

“Left.”

Left.

“Right.”

Right.

This time I did not argue.

Not because I trusted her.

Because arguing used time.

The turn still cost more than the left route.

But I made it without backing.

At the final opening she stepped into the lane.

I stopped.

Did not retreat.

Did not immediately turn either.

There was another opening two stakes behind my right shoulder.

I could get there.

Probably.

I shifted one crutch.

Pessa said, “No.”

I froze.

“What?”

“Stay.”

“For how long?”

She said nothing.

I stood.

This was stupid.

My palms were warming.

The right leg carried the center.

The phantom left foot felt planted half a step behind me.

It was not.

I knew it was not.

Knowing did not remove the sensation.

Pessa watched my shoulders.

Or hands.

Or feet.

Hard to tell.

Then she moved out of the lane.

“Go.”

I went straight.

Touched the mark.

“Why did you make me wait?”

“I wanted to see if waiting made you move.”

“That sentence is nonsense.”

“You move when you don't need to.”

I looked at her.

“When?”

“When you're trying to solve the next thing before it happens.”

That was dangerously close to sounding useful outside the yard.

I refused to allow it.

“In this yard.”

Pessa's mouth changed.

Barely.

“Yes. In this yard.”

Good.

We had rules.

Twenty minutes ended with me sitting on the low bench by the wall.

Palms hot.

Right calf working.

Residual limb still quiet.

Pessa untied the ropes.

I watched.

“You're not measuring anything?”

“I am.”

“Where?”

She tapped her forehead.

“That is unreliable.”

“So are you.”

“I could record the routes.”

“No.”

“Times.”

“No.”

“Number of corrections.”

“No.”

“Crutch contacts.”

“No.”

“Why not?”

She coiled the first rope.

“Because then tomorrow you'll arrive trying to improve the number.”

“That is the purpose of numbers.”

“Not mine.”

I considered arguing.

Theatre supplied an unwanted memory.

One run had been good.

I had tried to copy it.

The next had died.

I immediately became angry at my own brain.

No.

Pessa was not theatre.

This was not acting.

The similarity did not create a rule.

I looked at the dirt instead.

Pessa noticed.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“Good.”

Everyone in Carrow had apparently formed a conspiracy around that word.

She finished coiling the rope.

“Next time?”

I asked.

“Maybe.”

“That is not scheduling.”

“No.”

“Hessa tomorrow morning.”

Pessa looked at me.

“I didn't ask.”

“I know.”

“Then why tell me?”

“So you know I may not come.”

“I know you may not come every day.”

There was no accusation in it.

No lesson either.

Just fact.

I leaned back against the wall.

Across the yard, someone I did not know came through carrying two practice spears.

Pessa pointed toward the rack without looking at him.

He put them away.

She had other work.

Of course.

I stood.

“Done?”

“Yes.”

“Any objection to walking?”

“Can you walk?”

“Yes.”

“Then why are you asking me?”

“I hate this arrangement.”

“No, you don't.”

That was annoyingly accurate.

I left.

At the Guild, I did not immediately look for work.

This was unusual enough that I noticed.

I bought food instead.

Sat.

Ate.

Someone at the next table argued about freight rates.

Two Bronze adventurers I recognized but did not know were comparing cuts on a leather vambrace.

A clerk carried three bundles from one desk to another and dropped one.

Nobody needed me.

I drank water.

My palms cooled.

Right calf remained tired but ordinary.

Theatre was west.

I knew approximately what time rehearsal usually started now.

That was dangerous information.

Not dangerous.

Available.

I could go.

Nobody expected me.

Teren did not care.

The woman had not asked.

The servant actor would presumably survive without being told I liked him again.

I stayed at the Guild.

Not as a demonstration.

I was tired.

That was sufficient.

A clerk eventually stopped beside my table.

“Gregory?”

“Yes.”

“There is a receipt comparison if you want it.”

“How long?”

“Maybe an hour.”

“Seated?”

“Yes.”

I looked at the papers under his arm.

Ordinary work.

Suitable.

Paid, presumably.

I could do it.

That did not create a reason to.

“Not today.”

“All right.”

He walked away.

No disappointment.

No argument.

No consequence I could see.

This remained one of the stranger discoveries of the last few weeks.

A thing could fit my current capacities and still not become mine.

I drank more water.

Across the room, the dropped bundle had been gathered. The freight argument had changed participants. Someone opened the front door and let in a stripe of afternoon light that crossed the floor and stopped under an empty chair.

I knew theatre was west.

I knew work had just been offered here.

I knew I could probably find Lyssa if I wanted to spend the effort.

I knew Jorren might appear or might not.

Too many available choices should have felt like wealth.

Mostly they felt like having six doors and no sign over any of them.

I did not need a sign.

Annoying.

I remained seated.

Not as a demonstration.

I was tired.

That was sufficient.

After a while Jorren appeared, saw me, and changed direction.

He had a folded paper in one hand.

“Alive?”

“Yes.”

“Disappointing.”

He sat opposite me.

“What happened to you?”

“Pessa.”

“That explains the face.”

“What face?”

“The one where you're arguing with someone who isn't here.”

“I am not.”

“Good.”

I hated that word.

He unfolded the paper.

Not mine.

Not my business.

I did not ask.

This was apparently a day of miracles without magic.

Jorren looked at me.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You're staring.”

“I am practicing not asking.”

“Why?”

“Don't ruin it.”

He laughed.

We sat.

For several minutes, neither of us improved.

Eventually he left because he had somewhere else to be.

I remained because I did not.

The afternoon moved.

At some point, I realized rehearsal had probably begun.

I did not go.

At some later point, I realized it was probably still happening.

I still did not go.

No ache opened in my chest.

No sense of lost destiny.

No fear they would forget me.

They might.

That seemed reasonable.

I had been there yesterday.

I might be there another day.

Or not.

The thought did not become smaller because I stayed away.

Neither did Pessa's yard.

Neither did Hessa tomorrow morning.

This was getting crowded.

I went home before my right calf became an argument.

The keeper was at the desk.

She looked at my shirt.

Still not green.

“Not theatre.”

“No.”

“Where?”

“Pessa.”

She nodded as though this restored the natural order.

“It does not.”

“What?”

“Nothing.”

Upstairs, I sat in the chair by the window.

I considered the notebook.

Movement session.

Routes.

Blocks.

Wait.

Crutch slip.

Correction.

There were things worth recording.

I opened it.

Then stopped.

Pessa had not forbidden me to record my own body.

She had forbidden me to turn her yard into a score before I understood what she was looking at.

Probably.

I wrote:

PALMS HOT AFTER TWENTY MINUTES. RIGHT CALF TIRED. NO RESIDUAL-LIMB CHANGE. NO HAND SYMPTOM.

Then:

ONE RIGHT CRUTCH TIP BEGAN TO SLIDE ON LOOSE DIRT. FELT IT BEFORE FULL LOAD. UNLOADED AND RESET. NO FALL.

I stared at the page.

I wanted columns.

I did not draw them.

Tomorrow morning belonged to Hessa.

Today had belonged to Pessa for twenty minutes.

The rest had mostly belonged to me.

I had done almost nothing with it.

That was not true.

I had eaten.

Sat.

Talked to Jorren.

Not gone to theatre.

Come home before tired became stupid.

Very poor résumé.

Good day.

Probably.
CHAPTER 120
THE REPEATER

Hessa asked about the crutch before she asked about magic.

“Which one?”

“Right.”

“Tip slipped?”

“Began to.”

“Fell?”

“No.”

“Caught yourself?”

“I unloaded it before full weight.”

“With what?”

“The other crutch and right leg.”

She looked up.

“That is not what I meant.”

I knew.

“Hands?”

“Hot after training. Fine by later afternoon.”

“Calf?”

“Tired. Fine this morning.”

“Residual limb?”

“Baseline.”

“Thumb?”

“No.”

“Fingers?”

“No.”

“Any urge to move them?”

“No.”

“Forearm?”

“No.”

“Cold?”

“No.”

“Anything below the left knee that felt different from ordinary phantom sensation?”

“No.”

She wrote.

I sat on the same stool.

My right sleeve was already rolled above the elbow because experience had finally defeated ceremony.

Hessa noticed.

“Efficient.”

“I am capable of learning.”

“Occasionally.”

I looked at the tray.

Copper.

Charcoal.

Cloth.

Water.

Nothing else.

No object waiting to be affected.

No external-effect apparatus.

I had known there would not be.

Probably.

I was still disappointed.

That seemed unreasonable.

She had said closer.

Closer was a direction, not a destination.

I hated directions without distances.

Hessa finished writing.

“Yesterday was Pessa?”

“Yes.”

“And no magic.”

“Yes.”

“The day before?”

“Theatre. No magic.”

“After our last test?”

“No symptoms.”

“None you forgot to mention because they seemed unrelated?”

I thought.

This was a trap only if I deserved it.

“No.”

“Good.”

She closed the notebook.

“What do you think we're testing today?”

I did not answer immediately.

That was growth.

Or suspicion.

“Repeatability.”

“Too broad.”

“Whether I can reduce an alteration again while maintaining the underlying draw.”

“Better.”

“Without recruiting my hand.”

“Also relevant.”

“And without pushing the alteration somewhere else.”

“Relevant.”

“And whether I can tell when it is gone.”

She tilted her head.

“That one may be too ambitious.”

“Why?”

“Because last time you could not.”

“That is why we should test it.”

“That is why I am not making it the instruction.”

I disliked this.

“What is the instruction?”

“The same useful part as last time.”

“Same target?”

“Approximately.”

“Approximately is a new variable.”

“Yes.”

“That defeats repeatability.”

“No.”

“It changes location.”

“Barely.”

“Barely is not zero.”

Hessa took the charcoal.

“Gregory.”

“Yes.”

“I am not trying to prove you can reproduce a laboratory result.”

“We do not have a laboratory.”

“Then we agree.”

“That was not agreement.”

She drew a short line on the intact right forearm, near the wrist-side area she had used last time.

Not identical.

I could tell because I had stared at the previous mark for far too long.

“This is slightly farther inward.”

“Yes.”

“How much?”

“I did not measure.”

I stared at her.

She smiled.

Cruel woman.

“Why?”

“Because your arm is not a board.”

“It has dimensions.”

“So does bread. I do not use calipers before breakfast.”

“That is because bread is not mana.”

“Good. We have established one difference.”

I looked at the line.

“Instruction?”

“Minimal draw.”

“Then shape toward the line.”

“Yes.”

“How much?”

“Small.”

“Same as last time?”

“As close as you can without turning that into the task.”

Impossible sentence.

“And then?”

“I say RETURN.”

“One return?”

“One.”

“No refinement?”

“No.”

“If one edge remains?”

“You leave it.”

“If it shifts?”

“You tell me.”

“If I cannot tell?”

“You tell me that.”

“If reduction stops?”

“You tell me.”

“If I think I can improve it?”

“You do not.”

“That seems targeted.”

“It is.”

“At me.”

“Yes.”

Fair.

She moved the copper into place.

“Before we begin, hands.”

I opened and closed the right hand.

Normal.

She pressed along the forearm.

“Anything?”

“No.”

“Thumb?”

“No.”

“Good. Minimal draw only.”

I settled.

The first part had become familiar enough to be dangerous.

Not easy.

Familiar.

There was a difference.

I found the draw.

Small.

Supervised.

Nothing like Barrier.

Nothing completed.

No external movement.

Copper responded.

Hessa watched it.

“Hold.”

I held.

The phantom left foot existed because it usually existed.

Heel.

Toes.

A faint sense of the ankle being somewhere it was not.

Ordinary.

Not involved.

“Right forearm only,” Hessa said.

“Yes.”

“Toward the mark. Small.”

I shaped.

The alteration gathered near the charcoal line.

Narrower than the old broad pattern.

Not perfectly narrow.

I could feel the temptation to improve it before she said anything.

Do not.

That was not an instruction from Pessa.

Not theatre.

Not philosophy.

Hessa had literally told me not to refine.

Useful distinction.

“Hold.”

I held.

Copper response changed.

Hessa leaned slightly closer.

My fingers stayed open.

No urge.

No cold.

No thumb.

“RETURN.”

I stopped feeding the alteration and tried to reduce it while keeping the underlying draw.

At first, nothing obvious happened.

I waited.

No.

Not waited.

Continued the reduction.

The wrist-side edge softened.

Then the center.

The upper edge remained clearer.

Last time I had tried to fix that.

This time I did not.

It was irritating.

The upper edge persisted.

I could feel it.

Probably.

The rest diminished.

“Report,” Hessa said.

“Reduction. Wrist side first. Center dimmer. Upper edge remains.”

“Any movement?”

“No.”

“Urge?”

“No.”

“Continue RETURN. Do not correct the edge separately.”

I continued.

The upper edge dimmed.

Not smoothly.

It seemed to hold, then drop.

Copper diminished.

I felt the alteration become harder to distinguish.

This was where last time I had lost certainty.

I wanted to search.

Did not.

“Report.”

“Less.”

“Specific.”

“Upper edge less distinct. Center maybe still present.”

“Maybe?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

I hated when uncertainty earned approval.

“Continue.”

I did.

The alteration thinned further.

Or my ability to perceive it did.

Those were not the same.

I knew that.

Could not separate them.

“I cannot tell whether the center remains.”

“Do not search.”

“I know.”

“Then stop trying.”

“I am not.”

She looked at my face.

I stopped trying harder.

That sentence made sense only internally.

Probably.

“Maintain underlying draw.”

I did.

This was the strange part.

The draw remained.

The alteration was uncertain.

I could still tell those apart.

I thought.

KNOW versus THINK.

“I know the draw remains,” I said.

“Do you?”

“I am more confident of that than whether the alteration remains.”

“Better answer.”

Not yes.

Better answer.

Hessa watched the copper.

“Hold.”

I held.

My right hand stayed still.

No fingers.

No wrist.

No thumb.

The copper response stayed at the quieter level.

“Release.”

I released.

Everything settled.

Hessa immediately took my hand.

“Open.”

It was open.

“Close.”

I closed it.

“Again.”

Open.

Close.

Thumb.

Wrist.

She checked strength against her fingers.

“Any tingling?”

“No.”

“Cold?”

“No.”

“Numb?”

“No.”

“Pain?”

“No.”

“Urge?”

“No.”

“Left side?”

“Ordinary phantom foot.”

“Different?”

“No.”

She waited.

I waited.

Neither of us moved.

“This is where you tell me what happened.”

“I am deciding.”

“That is concerning.”

“It should be reassuring.”

“Not historically.”

She wrote first.

I tried to read upside down.

She moved the notebook.

“That is hostile.”

“It is medicine.”

“Those are not mutually exclusive.”

She finished the line.

Then looked at me.

“You reduced it again.”

“Yes.”

“While maintaining the draw.”

“Yes.”

“No observed shift toward the elbow.”

“Yes.”

“No motor urge.”

“Yes.”

“No separate correction.”

“Because you prohibited it.”

“Yes.”

“The remaining edge reduced when you continued the same RETURN instruction.”

“Yes.”

“And you again reached a point where you could not confidently distinguish residual alteration.”

“Yes.”

I waited.

She did not continue.

“That is three.”

“Three what?”

“Successful reductions.”

“No.”

“Ch111.”

“Different instruction and different observation.”

“Ch114.”

“Messy.”

“Ch117.”

“Yes.”

“Today.”

“Yes.”

“That is at least three.”

Hessa tapped the charcoal with one finger.

“You are counting categories I am keeping separate.”

“Why?”

“Because Ch111 was stop-feeding after ENOUGH. Ch114 was the first deliberate RETURN and included an unintended elbowward shift plus finger-curl urge. Ch117 was cleaner overall but you sharpened an edge when you tried to refine. Today I removed the refinement question and asked for one continuous reduction.”

“All are reduction.”

“All involve reduction.”

“That is what I said.”

“No. You said they are the same count.”

“I said three.”

“You are trying to make a score.”

I leaned back.

“I did not bring columns.”

“I am proud of you.”

“That sounded insulting.”

“It was mostly sincere.”

Mostly.

I looked at the fading charcoal line.

“So what did today answer?”

“That you can repeat the broad action under a slightly changed target without the two specific unwanted responses we saw before.”

“Broad action.”

“Deliberately reduce a small shaped alteration while keeping an underlying draw active.”

“That sounds less broad.”

“It is broad compared with precise control.”

“What would precise control be?”

“Not today's question.”

Of course.

“Does today increase confidence?”

“Yes.”

“How much?”

“No.”

“Hessa.”

“No.”

“Does it change external effect?”

“It changes my confidence in considering it.”

My attention sharpened.

“That is almost clearance.”

“No.”

“Scheduling?”

“No.”

“Then what changed?”

She looked at me for long enough that I regretted asking in that tone.

Then she answered anyway.

“I am less concerned that the moment you deliberately alter a draw, your only options are continue, lose the draw, or recruit some other pattern.”

I stopped.

That was more than I expected.

She continued.

“I have now seen you reduce an alteration while the draw remains. More than once. Under instructions that were not identical. Today you did it without the elbowward shift, without the finger urge, and without trying to repair the remaining edge separately.”

“So the next question is external.”

“No.”

I stared.

She stared back.

“You enjoy this.”

“I enjoy accuracy.”

“You enjoy accuracy when it hurts me.”

“That is still accuracy.”

“What is the next question?”

“Not today.”

“You know.”

“I have possibilities.”

“Which?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because then you will spend the next two days practicing a test you are not allowed to practice.”

“I cannot practice without mana.”

“You can rehearse decisions.”

That was offensive because it was true.

“I would only think about it.”

“Yes.”

“That is not practicing.”

She gave me the same look Pessa had given me yesterday when I suggested choosing the route she was less likely to block.

Apparently my face was becoming a liability across professions.

I changed direction.

“How many living days?”

“One.”

I blinked.

“One?”

“One full day. No magic.”

“Then return?”

“Yes.”

“Morning?”

“Yes.”

“That sounds almost like momentum.”

“It sounds like a schedule.”

“What symptoms change it?”

“Any thumb tingling. Any finger-curl urge. Any involuntary movement. New weakness. Cold. Numbness. Pain. Anything in the left-side phantom pattern that is distinctly unusual for you. Anything you think is probably nothing but are tempted not to tell me.”

“That last category is too broad.”

“It is tailored.”

I sighed.

“One day.”

“One.”

“That is shorter than last time.”

“Yes.”

“Because today was cleaner?”

“In part.”

“What is the other part?”

“You tolerated the previous interval without delayed symptom.”

“That sounds like progress.”

“It is information.”

“You have an allergy to the word progress.”

“I have an allergy to you using it as permission.”

“I can progress without permission.”

“Not in here.”

That was fair enough to be irritating.

I rubbed my thumb against the crutch grip, then realized I was checking it.

Normal.

Hessa noticed.

“Symptom?”

“No. Checking.”

“Stop checking.”

“That seems medically irresponsible.”

“Checking once because something feels wrong is useful. Checking every thirty seconds because you want certainty creates noise.”

I lowered my hand.

“You cannot possibly know I check every thirty seconds.”

“I know you.”

“That is not measurement.”

“No.”

She seemed completely comfortable with this.

“And then?”

“Assessment.”

“Not external effect.”

“I did not say that.”

I went still.

Hessa's expression changed immediately.

Not alarm.

Annoyance.

“Do not do that.”

“Do what?”

“Turn an omitted answer into permission.”

“I did not.”

“You absolutely did.”

“I observed that you did not exclude it.”

“That is not clearance.”

“I know.”

“Say it.”

“This is humiliating.”

“Good.”

I hated that word.

“External-effect testing is not cleared.”

“Or scheduled.”

“Or scheduled.”

“Casting?”

“Not cleared.”

“Barrier?”

“Not cleared.”

“Left shaping?”

“Excluded.”

“Independent draw?”

“Not allowed.”

“Independent shaping?”

“Not allowed.”

She nodded.

“Now you may be pleased.”

“I was already pleased.”

“That was the problem.”

She wiped the charcoal from my arm.

I watched the black line smear, then disappear under the damp cloth.

“Can I ask one question?”

“You have asked approximately forty.”

“One more.”

“You will ask it regardless.”

“Probably.”

She put the cloth down.

“What would make you decide not to test external effect?”

Her expression changed.

Small.

More serious.

“Several things.”

“Such as?”

“A delayed symptom.”

“Obvious.”

“A repeat control failure that looks meaningfully different from ordinary inconsistency.”

“Meaningfully how?”

“I will decide.”

I disliked that.

“Motor recruitment again?”

“Yes.”

“Broad familiar pattern?”

“Yes.”

“Loss of ability to release?”

“Yes.”

That one landed differently.

I had not lost release.

Not once.

Still.

“What else?”

“If I decide we do not yet understand enough about what you are doing to make an external question worth the added uncertainty.”

“External effect is added uncertainty.”

“Of course.”

“But isn't that the point?”

“No.”

I frowned.

“The point is to ask a question we can interpret.”

That was annoyingly good.

“If something happens externally but we don't know what internal change caused it, we learn less.”

“Yes.”

“If nothing happens externally, we may also learn less.”

“Depending on the test.”

“So you need internal control good enough that external failure or success means something.”

Hessa's mouth tightened.

I had gone too far.

Not wrong.

Too far.

“Approximately,” she said.

I wanted the rest.

I wanted the apparatus.

I wanted the exact threshold.

I wanted to know whether tomorrow's living day was the last ordinary day before something new.

No.

That was not available.

I put my sleeve down.

Hessa watched me do it.

“You can go.”

“That was abrupt.”

“The appointment is over.”

“I am accustomed to more resistance.”

“To leaving?”

“Yes.”

“That explains much.”

I stood.

Crutches.

Right hand normal on the grip.

Left.

Right foot.

No dizziness.

No symptom.

At the door I stopped.

Hessa sighed before I turned.

“I have not asked yet.”

“You stopped walking.”

“That is not a question.”

“It is with you.”

Fair.

“What should I do today?”

She stared.

Then pointed toward the door.

“Live.”

“That instruction remains poorly specified.”

“Excellent.”

Outside, Carrow was offensively normal.

A cart had lost part of a load of onions near the corner.

Three people were collecting them while a fourth argued about whose fault it was.

A dog had acquired one onion and seemed disappointed.

I stood there longer than necessary.

One living day.

Then Hessa.

Maybe external effect.

Not scheduled.

Not cleared.

Maybe another control test.

Maybe draw only.

Maybe nothing.

I could build a decision tree.

I did not have the notebook open.

That was the only thing preventing it.

I started toward the Guild.

Not theatre.

Not because I had decided against theatre.

It was morning.

Rehearsal, if they were rehearsing, would be later.

Pessa might be working.

Lyssa might be working.

Jorren was certainly doing something he would refuse to explain properly.

The Guild would contain work I could accept or decline.

Food.

People.

Nothing.

Options.

My right forearm felt ordinary beneath the sleeve.

That was becoming an achievement I did not know how to value.

At the Guild entrance, I paused.

A posting board had three new slips.

Someone I knew only by face was arguing with a clerk about a route.

Two people came out carrying packs.

The day was already happening.

Tomorrow had a rule.

Today did not.

I went inside.

For once, that was enough.
